title: Trade Deflection Index
text:
TDI
        Trade Deflection Index
      
      
        Monitoring the extent to which reduced Chinese exports to the U.S. market
        are offset by increased exports of the same products to third markets,
        since the introduction of new U.S. tariffs.
      
    
  







  
    About the Trade Deflection Index

    
      The Trade Deflection Index (TDI) measures the extent to which reduced exports to one
      tariff-imposing market are offset by increased exports of the same products to other
      foreign markets. It is the ratio of the increase in exports from China to third
      markets relative to the decrease in exports of the same products (at the HS6 level)
      to the U.S. market, using year-on-year changes calculated on three-month moving
      averages. In this pilot, the origin country is fixed as China and the
      tariff-imposing country is fixed as the United States.
    

    
      
        What does it measure?
        
          The Index is a simple metric of possible trade deflection and does not capture
          causal relationships — other structural and non-tariff factors could drive
          observed patterns. Trade deflection may still occur if imports are stagnant or
          growing more slowly. Index components can be aggregated across products and
          third countries to yield an overall estimate of total losses offset in foreign
          markets.
        
      
      
        How is it interpreted?
        
          A common global denominator is used so that group-specific index values can be
          interpreted as contributions to total offset. The upper bound estimate includes
          all trade flows that meet the index conditions; the lower bound estimate excludes
          changes below the 1st percentile or above the 99th percentile. Data are updated
          periodically subject to availability.

            Figure
            i
              How the selection works
              This figure breaks the deflection index down along two lines: geography (income → region → country) and industry (sector → product). You build a view by choosing values on either line.
              On each dropdown, leaving it on "select" ignores that level. Picking a single value filters the chart to it. Choosing "all" breaks the chart down into that level's parts (for example, all regions, or all sectors).
              Country and sector let you pick several at once to compare them side by side, up to ten. Picking "all sectors" shows the top ten in the current scope and offers the rest through download.
              One line can break down while the other filters — for instance, all regions within a single sector. The two lines cannot both break down at the same time, so the chart will ask you to narrow one.
              Choosing a single country sets its income and region for you; you can still change them.
